# Lock Code Manager

**Lock Code Manager scales down to a simple UI for managing your lock's PIN
codes — and scales up to a programmable, multi-lock, multi-provider PIN
platform with scheduled access, condition-driven activation, and
automation-ready services.** Define your codes once and LCM handles setting,
clearing, and monitoring them on every lock, across providers (Z-Wave, ZHA,
Matter, and more) without you wiring up the differences.

Whether you just want a clean dashboard for your front door or you're rotating
PINs across an Airbnb fleet on a nightly schedule, LCM has you covered.

Features:

- Give each person a name and a PIN; Lock Code Manager works out which slot
  on which lock they land in
- Synchronize PIN codes across multiple locks and providers
- Automatic sync — every write is read back from the lock to confirm it, with
  retries and drift detection
- Never touches codes it didn't create: a new user gets a slot number that's
  free on every lock in the configuration, and a lock you add or swap in later
  must have its users' numbers free, or it's refused until you clear them.
  Clearing or removing a user never deletes a lock user without Lock Code
  Manager's tag, and on Matter only PINs Home Assistant created are removed.
  The one exception is a lock that can't report its codes: Lock Code Manager
  warns you which slots it will use
- Shows what each lock reports for each slot, including when a lock can't tell
- [Repairs][wiki-repairs] tell you when a code can't be set or cleared, a lock
  is offline, or a lock was re-paired
- [Condition entities][wiki-conditions] control when a code is active: a
  calendar, a schedule, or anything on/off. Any other state, such as people
  being home, works through a template binary sensor
- [Services and actions][wiki-services] for managing users, PINs, and
  conditions from automations
- [Blueprints](BLUEPRINTS.md) for usage limiting, calendar-driven PINs, and more
- [External keypads and code readers][wiki-external-keypads], such as an
  ESPHome keypad, checked against the same users and schedules
- [Guest and rental workflows][wiki-guests]
- [Dashboard strategies and custom cards](#ui--dashboards), from one-line
  auto-generated dashboards to fully hand-composed layouts

I committed and pushed the screenshot and opened [PR #1799](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1799). The commit is `f2801099`, and the `prek` checks passed. Your main checkout is back on a clean `main`.

The screenshot won't show in the PR preview. The README links to it by its URL on `main`, so it only loads after the merge. The PR description says so, in case a reviewer asks.

I didn't check whether a Breaking Change section was needed: there isn't one, since nothing breaks. For "Type of change" I ticked "Code quality improvements", the closest of the template's options for a docs-only change.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.


Summary:
1. **Primary Request and Intent:**
   - The user first asked how to respond to a forum post: "how do I get the history of who unlocked which door and when?" The lock's activity shows "No cause was recorded", and the LCM card's "Last used" more-info dialog only shows "pin".
   - They then asked me to research a logbook feature, and later to "do A and C in one PR".
     - Option A: LCM writes a logbook entry on the lock it was used on.
     - Option C: the user card lists recent uses.
   - They asked whether A is a hack, and asked me to check the most popular custom integrations: analytics.home-assistant.io/custom_integrations.json, falling back to HA's GitHub analytics repo.
   - "go for it, also draft a new reply based on the assumption that we are building this".
   - "show me a mock of what the new card will look like".
   - "then run code review on this PR".
   - They asked whether the drafted forum post was accurate (they had struck out the workaround with an EDIT).
   - They said the context propagation "shouldn't be a follow up. We should do a third review after".
   - "run review one more time" (fourth review).
   - "embed ~/Downloads/all-locks.png in the README", then "yes" to committing and opening a PR.

2. **Key Technical Concepts:**
   - **Logbook filtering:** per-entity logbook queries (`async_determine_event_types`) include custom described events only from the integrations that own the queried entity. A `logbook.py` describing LCM's event never reaches a lock's activity view. The query matches an `entity_id` or `device_id` key in the event data.
   - **`logbook_entry`:** `EVENT_LOGBOOK_ENTRY` (what `logbook.log` and `async_log_entry` fire) is included for any entity named in its `entity_id`.
   - **Frontend never shows the entry's `name`** when `entity_id` is set. `logbook-entry-model.ts:404` uses `display?.primary ?? entry.name`, and `ha-more-info-logbook.ts` uses `name-detail="none"`. The person's name must go in the message.
   - **Cause comes from shared context IDs.** Pass `call.context` from `use_credential`. Never borrow the lock's own context.
   - **`history/stream` vs `history/history_during_period`:** the stream subscribes first, sends history, waits for the recorder commit, sends uncommitted rows, then streams live states with attributes. A one-off read misses uses not yet committed.
   - **Precedent:** no core integration writes `logbook_entry`. Of the top 92 custom integrations (repos mapped through data-v2.hacs.xyz/integration/data.json), only Better Thermostat does, and only on its own entity. Alexa and HomeKit get credit through context instead.
   - **Repo:** layering (`sync/`, `model/`, `ha/`, `providers/`); `prek`; strict layer imports. The clean-room core is already merged (#1702), and the xfail-only rule ended on 2026-10-26.
   - **HACS:** `render_readme: true`, so README images must use absolute raw.githubusercontent URLs.

3. **Files and Code Sections** (worktree `/Users/raman/projects/lock_code_manager/.worktrees/credential-use-logbook`, branch `feat/credential-use-logbook`, PR #1796, head `8bf99715`):
   - **`custom_components/lock_code_manager/model/events.py`**
     - Added `_LOGBOOK_MESSAGE = "message"`, `_CREDENTIAL_PHRASES` (pin "a PIN", rfid "an RFID tag", fingerprint "a fingerprint", face "face recognition", password "a password", nfc "an NFC tag"), and `_OPERATION_PHRASES` (UNLOCK "Unlocked", LOCK "Locked").
     - `credential_use_message(name, credential_type, operation)` returns `"{done} by {name} with {credential}"`, or `"{name} used {credential}"` when the operation is unknown. It uses `_CREDENTIAL_PHRASES.get(credential_type, str(credential_type))` as a fallback.
     - `async_fire_credential_used(..., context: Context | None)`: `context` is a required keyword. It fires the bus event with `context=context`, then:
       ```python
       hass.bus.async_fire(EVENT_LOGBOOK_ENTRY, {ATTR_NAME: name, _LOGBOOK_MESSAGE: credential_use_message(...), ATTR_DOMAIN: DOMAIN, ATTR_ENTITY_ID: target}, context=context)
       ```
     - Imports come from `homeassistant.const`. There is no logbook import, and the manifest is unchanged from main (the `logbook` after-dependency was removed).
   - **`ha/services.py`:** `async_use_credential(..., context: Context, ...)` passes `context=context`. Imports `Context`.
   - **`__init__.py`:** `_use_credential` passes `context=call.context`.
   - **`providers/_base.py`:** `async_fire_code_slot_event` passes `context=None`, with a comment that sharing the lock's context would say the unlock caused the use.
   - **Tests updated with `context=None`:** `tests/test_event.py` and `tests/providers/zwave_js/test_e2e.py`.
   - **`tests/test_logbook.py`** (new):
     - Uses the real recorder and logbook, via a `recorder_db_url` autouse override and `hass.config.components.add("frontend")`.
     - Queries `logbook/get_events` by `entity_ids`.
     - Covers: a lock-observed use ("Unlocked by test2 with a PIN"); a reported use against `cover.side_gate` ("test1 used a PIN"), with no entry under the source; an automation whose `context_event_type == "automation_triggered"` and `context_entity_id == "automation.side_gate_keypad"`, and whose bus event context matches the run's context.
     - Exhaustive parametrized message test, an unworded kind "palm" producing "Unlocked by Alice with palm", and a no-two-kinds-read-the-same test.
   - **`ts/credential-uses.ts`** (new):
     - `CREDENTIAL_USE_LIMIT = 10`, a 30-day window, `CompressedState` and `CredentialUse` interfaces, and `OPERATION_LABELS`.
     - `buildCredentialUsesStream(entityId)`: `history/stream` with `include_start_time_state: false`, `minimal_response: false`, `no_attributes: false`, `significant_changes_only: true`.
     - `HistoryStreamMessage`, plus `isUse` (the state is a timestamp and `a.target` is a string).
     - `mergeUseRows(kept, incoming)`: dedupes by time with the later row winning, sorts newest first, and caps at the limit.
     - `toCredentialUses(rows, states)`: uses the target's friendly name, falling back to the entity ID, and never reads the source.
     - `describeCredentialUse(use, formatKind)`: returns "Kind · Unlocked".
   - **`ts/credential-uses.test.ts`:** unit tests for the above.
   - **`ts/slot-card.ts`:**
     - State: `_usesExpanded`, `_useRows?: CompressedState[] | null`, and `_usesStream?: {entityId; unsub?}` (compared by identity).
     - The event row has `aria-expanded` and no `aria-label`; clicking it calls `_toggleUses`.
     - `_renderUses` shows "Loading…", "Couldn't read the history", or "No uses in the recorded history", then rows plus a "Full history" button (calls `_navigateToEventHistory`, which opens more-info). It uses `formatKind` via `hass.formatEntityAttributeValue(eventState,'event_type',kind)`.
     - `_openUses` subscribes through `connection.subscribeMessage`. If it can't, it sets `_useRows = null`.
     - `_closeUses` runs on collapse, on `setConfig` user change, on `disconnectedCallback`, and when `_handleSubscriptionData` sees a different `event_entity_id`; in that last case it also collapses.
   - **`ts/ha_type_stubs.ts`:** optional `formatEntityAttributeValue?`.
   - **`ts/slot-card.styles.ts`:** `.uses`, `.use-row`, `.use-target`, `.use-kind`, `.use-time`, `.uses-message`, `.uses-full-history`.
   - **`ts/slot-card.dom.test.ts`:** `mountWithStreams` uses a fake `subscribeMessage` that routes `history/stream`. Covers: listing, live rows, collapse/unsub, disconnect unsub, user switch, slot names someone else (closes), late message from a closed stream ignored, and stream failure.
   - **`ts/slot-card.integration.test.ts`:** click expands, the full-history link dispatches `hass-more-info`, the a11y test, and the Enter/Space toggle.
   - **Docs and build:** `README.md` (Code Events paragraph: "Unlocked by Alice with a PIN" and the card list), `AGENTS.md` (data-flow note and Slot Card "Recent uses" bullet), and the rebuilt `www/generated/lock-code-manager.js`.
   - **README PR #1799** (branch `docs/readme-dashboard-screenshot`, commit `f2801099`):
     - `assets/all-locks.png` copied from `~/Downloads`.
     - In `README.md`'s UI & Dashboards section, after "...you want where you want it.":
       ```
       ![The auto-generated dashboard: a card per user with their PIN, condition, lock status and last use, and a card per lock showing which slots Lock Code Manager manages](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/main/assets/all-locks.png)
       ```
     - The main checkout was switched back to `main`, which is clean.
   - **Memory:**
     - Added `reference_ha_logbook_entry_display.md` and its MEMORY.md line.
     - Marked the handoff and xfail-rule memories historical/ended.
     - Saved a MemPalace drawer and a diary entry (`raman_projects` / `lock-code-manager`).

4. **Errors and fixes:**
   - **Stale memory:** I wrongly claimed the regression-net and clean-room freeze was still on. The user corrected me ("isnt the clean room core and regression net done?"), and I updated the memories.
   - **My first logbook.py suggestion was wrong** (domain gate). Research corrected it.
   - **Logbook test setup failed** because `hass_frontend` is missing. Fixed by marking `frontend` loaded.
   - **Pacing tests fail under `-n auto`.** They are load flakes; they pass serially.
   - **Lint errors:** no-continue, member-ordering, no-plusplus. Fixed. `prek` reformatting broke a string-replace edit, which I redid.
   - **Round 1 review:** fixed the commit race, flicker, pre-6.0 rows, label mismatch and the enum `==` check.
   - **A use vanished from the open list** after the current-state splice. Fixed, and later superseded by the stream.
   - **Round 2:** the frontend hides `name`, so the message now includes the person. Also: `setConfig` reset, re-expand caching, `formatEntityAttributeValue` instead of copied labels (and the contract test was removed), and dropping `aria-label`.
   - **The user insisted context must not be a follow-up.** I implemented it with an automation e2e test.
   - **Round 3:** five findings traced to the cache, so I switched to `history/stream`. Fired `EVENT_LOGBOOK_ENTRY` directly. Fixed comments.
   - **`sorted()` reordered the manifest** ("schedule"/"schlage"). Restored from origin/main.
   - **Round 4:** stream-identity guard, close (not reopen) when the slot changes hands, `significant_changes_only: true`, `toCredentialUses`, the KeyError fallback, the ISO acronym spelled out, and the PR body corrected.
   - **Forum workaround bug:** `name` is hidden, so the message must include the name.

5. **Problem Solving:**
   - Every change was mutation-checked. Final results: 3627 Python tests passed serially, 736 TypeScript tests passed, and `prek` was clean.
   - `yarn build` prints a pre-existing type error in `ts/generate-view.ts` (`pinActiveEntity`).
   - Copilot comments on #1796 were still pending.

6. **All user messages:**
   - "How do I respond to this forum post [post text about who unlocked which door, 'No cause was recorded', LCM dashboard Last used shows only pin]"
   - "Let's do research into that feature it seems useful"
   - "isnt the clean room core and regression net done?"
   - "lets do A and C in one PR. But is that a hack or do core integrations do this?"
   - "check the most popular custom integrations. They used to be availabile at analytics.home-assistant.io/custom_integrations.json but that may have changed with the change to move HACS to be the marketplace. If you can't find it there, check home-assistnat's github analytics repo"
   - "go for it, also draft a new reply based on the assumption that we are building this"
   - "what is the drafted response?"
   - "show me a mock of what the new card will look like"
   - "then run code review on this PR"
   - "is this accurate now? [pasted draft with struck-out workaround and 'EDIT: There isn't actually a good way to get the logbook to show these events without the integration doing it. So wait for the next release which will have it'] so I should correct the forum post? ?"
   - "is code review still running?"
   - "The logbook entry doesn't carry the context of the automation that triggered it. Both rounds flagged this; I've kept it as a follow-up. <- this shouldn't be a follow up. We should do a third review after"
   - "run review one more time"
   - Stop-hook MemPalace checkpoint feedback (system/hook, handled)
   - "embed ~/Downloads/all-locks.png in the README"
   - "yes" (commit and open PR)

7. **Pending Tasks:**
   - Copilot review comments on PR #1796, when they arrive. Per AGENTS.md: address or explain each, resolve them, summarize, and ask for confirmation before committing.
   - The user's forum post correction. I gave a corrected text with the new wording "Unlocked by Alice with a PIN" and a workaround template that puts the name in the message; the user posts it.
   - PR #1799 awaiting review and merge. The image only loads after merge.

8. **Current Work:**
   - I created PR #1799 (https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1799) embedding `assets/all-locks.png` in the README's UI & Dashboards section via an absolute raw URL. I used the PR template ("Code quality improvements" box), linked it with `link_pull_request`, and switched the main checkout back to `main`, which is clean.

content.text:
Main is green; its last run was today's scheduled Bombadil property tests. Every failing run is on an open Dependabot PR, and there are two causes.

**1. Hassfest fails on every PR, including any you open next.**
Home Assistant added a rule that a translation string can't have a placeholder inside single quotes. Two of our strings break it, in both `strings.json` and `translations/en.json` (lines 556 and 559):
- `exceptions.user_pin_not_unique.message`: `"'{name}': Another user already has this PIN."`
- `exceptions.user_pin_too_long.message`: `"'{name}': PIN may be at most 255 characters."`

Our code didn't change; the check got stricter. The Integration workflow fails at Hassfest. Each PR's Repository workflow then fails as well, because its Auto Merge job reports "Hassfest failed". That's why every Dependabot PR (#1801–#1809, #1795) shows both workflows red. Main stays green only because nothing has been pushed to it since the rule landed; the next push will fail too.

The fix is to drop the quotes, for example `"{name}: Another user already has this PIN."` or `"Another user already has this PIN ({name})."`, in both files.

**2. #1766, the Home Assistant group bump, can't install its dependencies.**
Pytest stops before running any tests: `zha==2.3.1` pins `zigpy==2.3.0`, but the bump requires `zigpy>=2.4.0`. Dependabot raised zigpy without raising zha to match, so this PR needs a manual fix or a fresh rebase from Dependabot. It's the same exact-pin problem as before.

Do you want me to open a PR that fixes the two strings? That would turn the Dependabot PRs green again once they rebase.
yes

| --- | --- | --- |
| PIN already taken | `'{name}': Another user already has this PIN.` | `{name} has a PIN another user already has.` |

The `FlakyStrategyDefinition` is covering a real assertion failure. During one example, the `loaded_slots_are_in_sync` invariant failed: user1's slot on `lock.test_1` (entry "Shared 1") didn't match its PIN `1357` after 8 sync ticks. Hypothesis then replayed the same steps to confirm the failure, and the replay went differently. That makes it report "Flaky" instead of the assertion. It also means CI printed no steps and no reproduction blob, which is why the step list you pasted is empty.

**What I found:**
- **It has happened once.** I checked every Integration run since Oct 27, on main and on branches. Pytest passed in all of them except two old blueprint-docs failures, which are since fixed. This is the first time this test has failed.
- **It doesn't reproduce locally.** I ran the machine four times under the CI profile (200 examples each, seeds 1–4) and all four passed.
- **#1810 didn't cause it.** That PR changes only two translation strings and the tests that match them, and Hassfest now passes on it.
- **The errors in the captured log are expected.** "Preparing lock … failed" and "Task exception was never retrieved" both come from failures the machine injects on purpose.
- **Something in the run depends on more than the generated steps.** A replay that behaves differently means that. The worker's timers use the event loop's clock, which the test's frozen clock controls, so they aren't it. The likeliest cause is work handed to background threads, which the harness waits for in real time. On a slower CI runner that could finish in a different order. I haven't confirmed this.
- **A test comment disagrees with the code.** The comment at `tests/properties/test_shared_lock_machine.py:245-248` says the fight window uses the real monotonic clock. The worker gets `clock=hass.loop.time` (`ha/runtime.py:299`), so fights do age out on the frozen clock. The test stays safe anyway, because it changes each slot at most `FIGHT_LIMIT - 1` times.

I've rerun the failed Pytest job on #1810. If it passes, #1810 can merge, and then the Dependabot PRs can be rebased.

If it recurs, it would be worth an issue. A slot that never gets back in sync is the kind of bug this machine exists to catch, and the race may be in the integration, not the test. Without a seed it's hard to chase, so the first step would be setting `derandomize=True`, or printing the seed in the `ci` profile, so a failure can be replayed.

The rerun failed the same way: user1's slot on `lock.test_1` never got back to `1357` within 8 sync ticks. Failing twice in the same place on #1810 makes this real, not a one-off. I still can't reproduce it locally.

**What I've ruled out:**
- **#1810's change.** It only edits two translation strings, and nothing in this test reads them.
- **Installed packages.** The passing Nov 2 run and the failing run installed the same 197 packages. The only difference is `mypy-extensions`, which the test doesn't use.
- **Python version.** The two failures ran 3.14.8 and 3.14.10; the pass ran 3.14.9.
- **A saved failing example being replayed.** CI doesn't keep Hypothesis's example database between runs, so each run explores from scratch.
- **Local reproduction on #1810's branch.** I ran all the property tests three times with coverage on, plus the machine alone once. Every test passed, and each run generated the full 200 examples, as on CI. (Those runs exited 1, but that was only the coverage floor, since the rest of the suite didn't run.)

Since #1796 merged, Pytest has passed five times and failed twice, both times on #1810. That fits a failure that depends on timing on CI's runners more than on which PR is running.

**Why it's hard to chase:** when the replay goes differently, Hypothesis reports `FlakyStrategyDefinition` and prints no seed, no steps and no reproduction blob. CI's log is also INFO-level only, so it doesn't show what happened to that slot.

**What I'd do next:** a small test-infrastructure PR that makes the next failure reproducible:
1. Pass `--hypothesis-seed` with a random value in the workflow and print it, so a failed run can be replayed locally with the same seed.
2. Turn on DEBUG logging for `custom_components.lock_code_manager.sync` in this machine, so the log shows each read, write and hold for the slot that stays out of sync.

Then rerun to get a seed and logs. If the failure is a real sync race, a slot staying out of sync on a lock shared by two entries is exactly the bug this test is meant to catch. I'd fix that separately, not inside the CI PR.

Until then, #1810 is held up only by this test. Hassfest passes on it. Do you want me to open the CI PR, or would you rather rerun #1810 again and merge it if it goes green?

content.text:
I don't have a fix yet. I opened a draft PR that should show what goes wrong on CI, and I'm waiting for its run.

**What changed:** the test now fails on main and on every Dependabot PR you merged or rebased, not just #1810. Every failure is identical: entry "Shared 1", user1, `lock.test_1`, PIN `1357`. That's the smallest case the test generates, one entry starting up on one lock. So on CI the most basic startup leaves a slot out of sync, while on my Mac the same case syncs every time.

**Ruled out:**
- The time zone: it passes locally under UTC, as CI runs.
- Which tests run before it.
- The Python patch version, the installed packages and #1810's change, as I found earlier.
- Random example choice: it passes locally even with Hypothesis set to generate the same fixed examples it would generate on CI.

So it depends on the environment, most likely timing on GitHub's runners. The last passing run was Nov 2, and it has failed since Nov 4.

**[Draft PR #1811](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1811)** (do not merge) runs the test on CI with two changes:
- **The same fixed examples as my local run.** If CI fails on them while my machine passes, that confirms the environment is the cause.
- **A report when the check fails.** The message now shows the worker's view of each slot (what it wants, what it last wrote and saw, retries, holds), the lock's real codes, each lock instance and how many times it was set up, read and unloaded, and the entity states. I forced a failure locally to check that this renders.

That report should show where the startup sync stalls: no read at all, a read nobody acted on, or a write that was held. Then I can fix that cause, not just the test.

I'm watching #1811 and will pick it up when its checks finish, in about 10 minutes.

test: each shared-lock machine example starts on empty storage, so CI stops failing it as flaky

Every example of the machine saved its registries into the one mocked store
the test's fixtures make, and the next example loaded them back. Where
ulid_transform falls back to pure Python, as on CI, entry IDs come from the
frozen clock and the global random, which Hypothesis seeds alike for every
example, so IDs repeat: an entry took over a device an earlier example had
disabled, its entities never got a state, and loaded_slots_are_in_sync
failed -- then passed on replay, reported as FlakyStrategyDefinition.

Each example now clears the store for itself, and asserts it starts with no
entities or devices, which catches the leak whichever ULID implementation
is installed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q -u origin fix/shared-lock-machine-storage-per-example 2>&1 | grep -v "^remote:\|entire"; gh pr create --title "test: each shared-lock machine example starts on empty storage, so CI stops failing it as flaky" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

`TestSharedLockMachine` has failed on main and on every PR since Nov 4 with `loaded_slots_are_in_sync`, reported as `FlakyStrategyDefinition`. It passed locally.

**Cause:** the test's autouse fixtures pull in `hass`, so one `hass_storage` mock serves all 200 examples. Each example's Home Assistant saved its device registry into that store, and the next example loaded it back. Where `ulid_transform` falls back to its pure-Python implementation, as it evidently does on CI, entry IDs come from the frozen clock and the global `random`. Hypothesis seeds that the same way for every example, so the IDs repeat. An entry then takes over a device that an earlier example had disabled. Its entities stay disabled with no state, and the slot never shows as in sync. The replay that follows passes, which Hypothesis reports as flaky.

With the compiled `ulid_transform` (macOS), every example gets new IDs, so the leaked devices never collide and the test passes. That's why it never reproduced locally. Forcing the pure-Python fallback reproduces CI's exact entry IDs and the same failure.

**Fix:** each example clears the shared store with `patch.dict(..., clear=True)` and asserts it starts with no entities and no devices. It can't use a nested `mock_storage()`, because `mock` won't autospec over the fixture's mock. The new assertion fails on both ULID implementations when the clear is removed, so the leak can't come back silently on either platform.

Verified locally, CI profile:

| | compiled ULID | pure-Python ULID |
| --- | --- | --- |
| with fix | pass | pass |
| without the clear | fail (`started with devices`) | fail (`started with devices`) |

input.content:
---
name: hypothesis-examples-share-fixture-storage
description: A Hypothesis state machine is one pytest test, so function fixtures (hass_storage via the autouse hass) span all its examples; registries leak between examples, and only collide where ULIDs repeat (pure-Python ulid_transform on CI)
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

`TestSharedLockMachine` failed on CI only (Nov 2026, fixed in #1812), reported as `FlakyStrategyDefinition`. Root cause: autouse `auto_enable_custom_integrations` → `hass` → one `hass_storage` mock for all 200 examples; each example's device registry was saved and loaded by the next. On macOS the compiled `ulid_transform` uses the real clock, so IDs never repeat and the leak is harmless. On CI the pure-Python fallback uses frozen `time.time` plus the global `random` (which Hypothesis reseeds alike per example), so entry IDs repeat and an entry adopts a device an earlier example disabled.

**Why:** cost several hours and two wrong theories (Python version, runner timing). A replay that diverges means the example depends on state outside it, so look for state that survives between examples first.

**How to apply:**
- Every example of a stateful machine must reset fixture-scoped state itself (`patch.dict(storage, clear=True)`; a nested `mock_storage()` fails because `mock` won't autospec over the fixture's mock), and assert a clean start (no entities, no devices).

- `derandomize=True` locally tells you whether a failure depends on inputs or on the environment.

I found the cause and opened the fix as **[#1812](https://github.com/raman325/lock_code_manager/pull/1812)**. It's a test bug, not a sync bug, and the test was failing for a real reason, not at random. It passes locally under both setups; CI hasn't run on it yet.

**Cause:** the shared-lock test runs all its examples inside one pytest test, so one mocked storage serves every example. Each example's Home Assistant saved its device registry there, and the next example loaded those devices back.

**Why only CI:** HA's ID library, `ulid_transform`, has a compiled version and a pure-Python fallback.
- On my Mac the compiled version uses the real clock, so every example gets new entry IDs and the leftover devices never match anything.
- CI evidently gets the pure-Python fallback, though I haven't confirmed why. It builds IDs from the test's frozen clock and from `random`, which Hypothesis seeds the same way for every example, so the same IDs come back each time.
- An entry then reused a device an earlier example had disabled. Its entities never got a state, and the in-sync check failed. When Hypothesis replayed the example to confirm, it passed, so it was reported as flaky.

Forcing the fallback locally produced CI's exact entry IDs (`01KDWPVNG9F3F591…`) and the same failure.

**The fix:**
- Each example clears the shared storage before it starts.
- Each example checks it starts with no entities and no devices.

| | compiled ID library | pure-Python fallback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| with the fix | pass | pass |
| fix removed | fail (`started with devices`) | fail (`started with devices`) |

So if the leak comes back, the test fails on any machine. All property tests pass locally under the CI profile.

I closed the diagnosis draft #1811 and deleted its branch, and saved a memory about this trap for future stateful tests. I'm watching #1812's CI and will pick it up when its checks finish. Once it merges, the Dependabot PRs need a rebase.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Hassfest rule:** translation strings may not contain placeholders inside single quotes (`'{name}'`).
   - **Hypothesis stateful testing:** `RuleBasedStateMachine` runs as one pytest test (one `runTest`), so function-scoped and autouse fixtures span all its examples.

   - **`ulid_transform` implementations:**
     - The compiled `_ulid_impl` uses the real C clock, which freezegun can't patch, so IDs are unique across examples.
     - The pure-Python `_py_ulid_impl` uses `from time import time` (frozen by freezegun) and `random.getrandbits` (reseeded identically per example by Hypothesis), so entry IDs repeat across examples. CI evidently uses this fallback.
   - **HA device registry:** with a repeating ID, `async_get_or_create` reuses a leftover device with `disabled_by=config_entry`, so its entities are `disabled_by=device` and have no state.

The repo is in good shape. `main` is green, with #1812 and the Dependabot batch merged, and only one PR is still open. What's left:

**Needs action now**
- **#1766, the Home Assistant group bump from Dependabot.** It's the one open PR, and Pytest fails on it at install, before any test runs. The bump moves zha to 2.3.1, which requires zigpy==2.3.0, but the same bump asks for zigpy>=2.4.0. Rebasing won't fix it. It needs one of these:
  - hold zha back,
  - leave zigpy at the version zha requires,
  - or wait for a zha release that allows zigpy 2.4.

**Open feature requests (4 issues)**

| Issue | Status |
|---|---|
| #1768 Group as a condition | Waiting on the reporter. You turned down presets and asked for a way that uses existing Home Assistant features. Template entities already do this, so it may simply close. |
| #1739 Per-lock slot numbers | Researched, with your design decisions still pending. Most of the work is config, identity and allocation; the sync engine already works per lock. This is the largest real feature still open. |
| #858 Alarm panel codes | Answered, since the Ring keypad and Alarmo setup works today through the existing code-event path. Native panel support isn't planned because Home Assistant has no code-level API for panels, so this could probably be closed. |
| #830 RFID per slot | Blocked behind the paused password and credential-types work. None of the supported locks accepts passwords yet, so that work stopped at #1769. |

**Parked work from my notes (not checked against the code today)**
- **Credential types.** Adding password support, and later RFID/NFC, is on hold until a supported lock can use them.
- **A loose end in the CI flake fix.** CI ends up with the pure-Python `ulid_transform` instead of the compiled one, and we never found out why. #1812 makes the test immune to it, but anything else that assumes unique IDs under a frozen clock could hit the same problem.

**Suggested order:**
1. Unblock #1766, since it holds back all the Home Assistant updates.
2. Close #858, and #1768 too if the reporter accepts template entities.
3. Make the #1739 design decisions, because that's the next real feature.

---

description: "#1739 per-lock slot numbers researched 2026-10-26; findings in docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-26-per-lock-slots-1739-research.md; identity decision pending"

Researched 2026-10-26; no design approved yet. Full findings with file:line are in
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-26-per-lock-slots-1739-research.md` (local only).

Headline: the sync engine (worker, registry, store, providers) is already per lock. The cost
sits in the config/HA layer (~85 functions), allocation (largest design piece) and the meaning
of `code_slot` for users. The user's number is both its registry identity and "the slot on
this lock". The upgrade copies the number onto every lock, so tests must use position ≠ number
or every misclassified site stays hidden. No user has reported the limits #1739 removes.

**Why:** Raman asked whether #1739 should headline 8.0.0. I advised against it: 8.0.0 is
already justified by #1774 and #1781, and #1739 needs its own design starting from identity.

**How to apply:** don't relitigate the research. Start from the open decisions in the doc
(identity option a/b/c1/c2, same-number preference, unreadable-lock behaviour). Related:
[[project_slot_number_is_two_keys_fused]] (its reuse reasoning stops holding under per-lock
slots), [[project_v3_migration_one_way_door]].
### Problem Description

Each user holds one slot number (`CONF_SLOT`) that is used on every lock in the configuration. Lock Code Manager picks it when the user is added, as a number free on all of the configuration's locks at that moment. That shared number causes the hardest limits left in the "you don't pick slots" design:

- **Allocation needs a number free on every lock.** The more locks in a configuration, and the more unmanaged codes they hold, the fewer numbers qualify.
- **Adding a lock is refused** (`existing_codes`) when the new lock already holds codes at numbers the configuration's users hold. The numbers were issued before the lock joined, and renumbering a user would mean rewriting their code on every other lock.
- **A smaller lock constrains the configuration** (`slot_out_of_range`): a user on slot 30 can't be added to a 20-slot lock even if it has free slots.

### Feature Description

Give each user a slot number **per lock** instead of one shared number.

The 7.0 engine is already per lock, so most of the stack needs no change:

- one `LockWorker` per lock with its own slot table (`sync/worker.py`);
- the `lock_code_manager.core` store is keyed per lock;
- queries already take a lock: `slots_configured_on(hass, lock)`, `configured_owner(hass, lock, slot)`;
- tags (`lcm:<slot>:`), events and attribution are read per lock;
- Matter already decouples the slot from the device credential index, and Akuvox/Schlage have no indices at all (the slot only lives in the tag).

What would change:

- **Config:** a user holds `{lock: slot}` instead of `CONF_SLOT`, with a migration that copies today's number onto every lock (no lock-side change on upgrade).
- **Allocation:** pick a free slot per lock; adding a lock picks free slots on that lock instead of refusing with `existing_codes`; `slot_out_of_range` goes away.
- **Lookups:** "user on lock" replaces "slot" as the key in `model/config.py`, `model/queries.py`, `config_flow.py`, `__init__.py` (`CONF_SLOT` is read in ~17 places).
- **User-visible surfaces built on "slot N":** event entity `code_slot` attribute and slot-based automations, the lock codes card's per-slot rows, the user card, the duplicate check across entries (`slots_already_configured`), diagnostics, and the slot section strategy.

### Anything else?

- Risk is mostly in the migration and in automations that assume the same `code_slot` on every lock; this needs its own upgrade note.
- A user's slot number could still default to the same

72	  notifier pairing `slot_num` with `lock_name`; calendar blueprints given a number copied off
73	  the lock codes card; legacy-mode grouping if unique IDs are re-keyed; the wiki's "stable,
74	  same position on every lock" claims.
75	- D, only if the configuration-wide key is dropped (~5): dashboard/view `condition_helpers`
76	  keyed by number; `slot:` on `lcm-user`/`lcm-slot`; the slot section strategy's `slot`; the
77	  calendar blueprints' `slot_number` and numbers in calendar event text; user automations on
78	  `code_slot`. LCM cannot migrate any of these.
79	
80	## Config, flows, migration
81	
82	- 17 `CONF_SLOT` references (listed in the identity trace).
83	- Migration v5→v6 writes `{lock: CONF_SLOT}` into each user subentry. No lock-side change.
84	  Needs a MAJOR entry version: HA refuses to load a newer version (`config_entries.py:1170-1179`),
85	  so this is a one-way door like v3.
86	- Traps:
87	  - `from_entry` strips only `CONF_SLOT` (`model/config.py:208-210`).
88	  - reconfigure replaces data wholesale (`config_flow.py:1377-1382`).
89	  - the edit form filters only `CONF_SLOT` (`:1404`).
90	  - `with_user_renamed` re-keys the assignment (`model/config.py:363-366`).
91	  - `has_changes` ignores a slot move on one lock, and the listener returns early
92	    (`model/config.py:574-581`, `__init__.py:2000-2007`), so the old address is never released.
93	  - nothing follows a lock entity rename into `CONF_LOCKS`; key the per-lock map by registry id
94	    like the store does.
95	- Options and reauth flows save only locks today (`config_flow.py:1104-1129`, `:259-293`). With
96	  per-lock slots they become allocating writers of every user subentry.
97	- Checks that go away or change: `existing_codes` (`config_flow.py:233-256`) becomes allocation
98	  on the new lock; `slot_out_of_range` goes; `numbers_needed_exceed_capacity` becomes per lock;
99	  `slots_already_configured` (`:184-210`) is no longer needed.
100	
101	## Allocation
102	
103	Today all locks are folded together: the smallest `async_max_slot` (`ha/allocation.py:398`),
104	unioned occupancy (`model/occupancy.py:67-69`), one window (`:474-525`), one held set
105	(`model/slot_assignment.py:119-130`). Per lock: one window per lock returning
106	`{lock: unavailable}`, and `SlotAssignment` as name → {lock: slot}. About 200-300 of ~880 lines.
107	
108	Decisions:
109	1. Prefer the same number on every lock (re-couples the searches) or take the lowest free slot per lock.
110	2. An unreadable lock (`occupancy_unknown`, `:488-493`): refuse everything as today, or allocate on the readable locks and defer.
111	
112	## Size
113

115	- Engine: small (queries ~40 lines, runtime ~50, coordinator ~60, store ~10, attribution ~5).
116	- Allocation: the largest design piece.

# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by understanding the current project context, then ask questions one at a time to refine the idea. Once you understand what you're building, present the design and get user approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any project, or take any implementation action until you have presented a design and the user has approved it. This applies to EVERY project regardless of perceived simplicity.
</HARD-GATE>

## Anti-Pattern: "This Is Too Simple To Need A Design"

Every project goes through this process. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config change — all of them. "Simple" projects are where unexamined assumptions cause the most wasted work. The design can be short (a few sentences for truly simple projects), but you MUST present it and get approval.

## Checklist

You MUST create a task for each of these items and complete them in order:

1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer visual companion** (if topic will involve visual questions) — this is its own message, not combined with a clarifying question. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Visual questions ahead?" [shape=diamond];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];

    "Explore project context" -> "Visual questions ahead?";
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" [label="yes"];
    "Visual questions ahead?" -> "Ask clarifying questions" [label="no"];
    "Offer Visual Companion\n(own message, no other content)" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**The terminal state is invoking writing-plans.** Do NOT invoke frontend-design, mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. The ONLY skill you invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans.

## The Process

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Key Principles

- **One question at a time** - Don't overwhelm with multiple questions
- **Multiple choice preferred** - Easier to answer than open-ended when possible
- **YAGNI ruthlessly** - Remove unnecessary features from all designs
- **Explore alternatives** - Always propose 2-3 approaches before settling
- **Incremental validation** - Present design, get approval before moving on
- **Be flexible** - Go back and clarify when something doesn't make sense

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion:** When you anticipate that upcoming questions will involve visual content (mockups, layouts, diagrams), offer it once for consent:
> "Some of what we're working on might be easier to explain if I can show it to you in a web browser. I can put together mockups, diagrams, comparisons, and other visuals as we go. This feature is still new and can be token-intensive. Want to try it? (Requires opening a local URL)"

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Do not combine it with clarifying questions, context summaries, or any other content. The message should contain ONLY the offer above and nothing else. Wait for the user's response before continuing. If they decline, proceed with text-only brainstorming.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

content.text:
All four decisions are recorded. Now the design, one section at a time.

## Section 1 of 4: Data model and migration

**Two types, so the meanings can't be mixed up:**
- `UserNumber`: the configuration-wide identity. It's issued once per user and never reused.
- `LockSlot`: a position on one lock.

Both are `NewType`s over `int`, so mypy flags any place that passes one where the other belongs. The research found a dozen such places in today's code.

**Storage:**
- Each user subentry keeps `CONF_SLOT` as its `UserNumber`, so there's no registry migration and every unique ID, device and `slot:` key stays the same.
- Each user subentry gains `lock_slots: {lock registry id: LockSlot}`. The map is keyed by entity registry id, as the core store already is, so renaming a lock entity's ID doesn't orphan the slot.
- The entry stores `next_user_number`, which only ever goes up, so numbers aren't reused. Today's reuse logic in `model/slot_assignment.py` goes away.

**Queries in `EntryConfig`:**
- Positions come from `slot_on(user, lock)`.
- `user_at(lock, slot)` replaces the uses of `has_slot` and `slot_numbers` that were really asking a position question. The research lists them at `model/queries.py:131,205` and `ha/runtime.py`.
- `slot_numbers` is renamed to `user_numbers`, so each remaining caller has to state which meaning it wants.

**Migration v5 → v6, a major entry version:**
- Each user gets `lock_slots = {lock: CONF_SLOT}` for every lock in the configuration, and `next_user_number` is set to the highest existing number plus one.
- Nothing is written to any lock, and every slot ends up where it already was.
- It's a one-way door like v3: Home Assistant won't load a v6 entry on an older Lock Code Manager, so the release notes have to say a downgrade means restoring a backup.

**Two traps from the research to deal with:**
1. Reconfigure replaces the entry data wholesale (`config_flow.py:1377-1382`), so it has to carry `next_user_number` across.
2. `has_changes` has to count a slot that moved on one lock as a change (`model/config.py:574-581`). Otherwise the old position is never released.

Does this section look right?
what is the benefit of this? less likely to refuse an allocation is the main benefit i think?

Yes, that's essentially the whole benefit: fewer refusals. Specifically, it removes three of them.

1. **Adding a lock** fails with `existing_codes` when the new lock already has codes in slots this configuration's users hold. With per-lock slots, those users would just get other free slots on that lock.
2. **A smaller lock** caps the configuration (`slot_out_of_range`). A user in slot 30 can't be added to a 20-slot lock, even if it has free slots.
3. **Adding a user** needs a slot that's free on every lock at once. The more locks there are, and the more codes Lock Code Manager doesn't manage, the fewer slots qualify. Eventually it refuses even though each lock has room.

Weighed against the cost:
- **Nobody has reported hitting any of them.** When I researched this, I searched for those error keys and the capacity errors and found no reports. The only related case, #865, was handled with overlapping configurations that each use their own slot range.
- **It's a big, one-way change.** It's comparable in size to the 5.0 and 6.0 migrations: about 85 functions in the config and Home Assistant layer, allocation rework, about 15 wiki pages, and a v6 entry version that can't be downgraded.
- **It costs some clarity.** "Slot 5 is Alice on every lock" is easy to explain and easy to check in Z-Wave JS UI or on a keypad. Per-lock slots trade that for two numbers, a user number and a lock slot, which you'd have to explain in the docs and on the cards, and which tests would have to keep apart forever.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The engine already works per lock, which made this look cheap. But the hard part was never the engine: it's that one number does two jobs, identity and position. Splitting them is right in principle, but nobody is hitting the problem.
- All three refusals are loud and happen at setup time, never as silent data loss. Users can see them and work around them, which makes them low-urgency.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**My recommendation is to park #1739.** I'd keep the decisions we just made in the research doc, so the design is ready, and label the issue as waiting for a real report of one of these three refusals. If you'd rather make some of it better now, the cheapest step is clearer refusal messages, not the restructure:
- For `existing_codes`, say which slots conflict and that clearing them on the lock fixes it.
- For a user who can't be placed, point to overlapping configurations as the workaround.

Do you want to park it, or go ahead anyway?
lets park 1739 and implement the clearer refusal messages
Parking #1739 first, then I'll look at the current refusal messages.

Allocation can tell which lock each blocking slot is on: each read returns per-lock results (`LockOccupancy`, one per lock), and they're only merged into one set by `Occupancy.unavailable`. So the fix is cheap. Here's the proposal.

**The change:**
1. Allocation searches in passes. As it goes, it would also keep each lock's occupied slots and the slots claimed by other configurations, both limited to the slots it searched.
2. `numbers_needed_exceed_capacity` would get a `{blocking}` placeholder that lists them grouped by lock, for example:
   > Placing 4 users would need slot numbers up to 24, and lock Front Door has 20 PIN code slots. These slots already hold codes: **Front Door 3, 7; Back Door 12, 15; another configuration 9**. Clearing codes nobody uses frees those slots. Otherwise, set up fewer users here, or manage the rest from a separate configuration. If the lock really does have more slots than that, re-interview it…
3. The other wording stays as it is. The same key is used in two places in `strings.json` (the config step and the add-user subentry), so both get the change, along with `en.json`.

**Tests:**
- An allocation test where the codes in the way are on two different locks, asserting the `blocking` placeholder itself, not text from the log. The test would sit next to the existing `numbers_needed_exceed_capacity` tests.
- A mutation check: merging the per-lock data back into one set must fail that test.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The merge in `Occupancy.unavailable` is deliberate. Allocation only needs "which numbers can't be issued", so the per-lock detail is dropped once it's no longer needed. - The message should list only slots the search actually covered. Listing every code on the lock would point users at codes that aren't in the way.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

This is the second pass. The first ([[project_v3_diff_size_question]], PR
#1439) swept comments and found that **45% of every source line v3 added was
prose** -- 747 of 1664. This pass is about structure rather than commentary.

## What to look for

* Indirection: helpers with one caller, wrappers that only rename, constants
  that exist to be passed to one function.
* Abstraction leaks: private names imported across module boundaries (found
  `_identity` imported from `slot_assignment` by `config` and two test
  modules), options that only ever take one value.
* Over-abstraction: parameters no caller varies, branches guarding conditions
  a later increment made impossible, projections kept "for now".
* Whole features whose cost exceeds their payoff -- see the precedent below.

## The precedent that justifies the pass

The automations auto-fixer (#1441) was scaled back to reporting-only in #1443
after four review rounds each found a NEW way it could damage a user's
configuration (`!include` flattened, `!secret` leaked/skipped, key collision
destroying an entry, chained double-apply, failed write reported as success).
It shrank 116 statements to 61. Nothing was lost that users wanted; the value
was in the reporting, and the risk was all in the writing.

Raman proposed the scale-back from less detail than I had. That is now 4/4 in
one session -- see [[feedback_simplicity_pushback_is_a_design_signal]].

## Method note

Measure before defending. The first pass answered the diff-size question by
counting what the diff spends lines on, not by arguing it was justified.

content.text:
I checked the main claims myself. Three are confirmed, and there's some useful history:

- **The reauth/options drift is real.** Options passes only newly added locks to `_check_common_slots` (`config_flow.py:1041`), and its comment explains why. Reauth passes every lock (`:911`). So an overlap with another configuration that options deliberately tolerates still blocks reauth.
- **The `source=` flag is only ever `"sync"` in production.** The adapter passes `source="sync"` (`ha/adapter.py:412`), and only Matter reads the flag (`matter.py:1674`).
- **Several findings were proposed before and never done.** `docs/superpowers/plans/simplify-plan.json` (Oct 16) lists 38 items that survived a critique. Most describe code from before the clean-room rebuild and no longer apply. Three are still open: `one-lock-change-validator` (the reauth/options merge), `ws-from-config-and-worker`, and `write-result-vestigial`, which already called for deleting `source=`.

## What's worth doing

**A. Inconsistencies that can go wrong for users. Fix these whatever we decide about the rest.**
1. **Reauth rejects a slot overlap that options accepts** (`config_flow.py:905` vs `:1028`). Merging both into one lock-change checker fixes the drift and removes about 45 duplicated lines.
2. **A user name is matched two different ways.** The websocket path compares names with `slugify` (`websocket.py:242`), while services compare them by stripping and case-folding (`services.py:132`). The same name can therefore resolve on one path and fail on the other.
3. **The duplicate-name check in the config flow** (`config_flow.py:503`) only case-folds; the YAML path also strips spaces. Fixing it is one line.

**B. Cheap, low-risk deletions (about 150 lines in total):**
- Remove the `source=` parameter (9 signatures) and Matter's unreachable `"direct"` branch.
- The stand-in coordinator in `ha/adapter.py` makes the first-read timeout and error block in `_base.py:805-826` impossible to reach.
- Copies that duplicate an existing builder or helper:
  - the unique-ID format is rebuilt by hand three times in `websocket.py`, though `model/config.build_slot_unique_id` exists;
  - `_slot_from_seam_user` is copy-pasted between Z-Wave JS and Matter;
  - two type-check helpers have identical bodies;
  - `CODE_SLOT_SCHEMA` duplicates `USER_SCHEMA` instead of extending it.
- Dead pieces:
  - attributes that are never read (`self.ent_reg`/`self.dev_reg` in `config_flow.py`, `self._hass` in `entity.py`);
  - a guard that's always true (`__init__.py:2117`);
  - the redundant zigbee2mqtt `supports_code_slot_events` override.
- The websocket entry lookup (`websocket.py:303`) is a copy of `get_loaded_config_entry`, and it skips the domain check, so passing another integration's entry ID crashes it.

**C. Medium consolidations (they touch many test mocks):**
- The coordinator's `push_update` and `observe_push` do the same thing; about 88 test references would change.
- The slot-keyed copies of the condition functions in `services.py` could be removed.
- Two provider factories could be merged into one.
- Three private provider members used from `ha/` could be made public.

**D. Your call. These are intentional future-proofing:**
- `_project_users_to_slots(credential_type)` is only ever called with PIN; it's an intentional extension point for the parked password work.
- `supports_code_slot_events` is overridden in 5 providers, but only diagnostics reads it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- All of section A are duplicates that have drifted apart, and that pattern caused real bugs earlier in this project. Removing duplicates matters mainly because it stops copies from drifting into different behavior; the line count is secondary.
- The dead code in B comes from earlier redesigns. When the rebuild replaced the coordinator with a stand-in whose values never change, the error handling that depended on it was left behind and can no longer run. Coverage didn't flag it because the lines still execute; only the branches can't happen.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

My suggestion is two PRs:
1. **Section A as a bug fix** ("reauth no longer refuses an overlap that options accepts", plus the two name-matching fixes).
2. **Section B as one cleanup PR.**

C and D can wait. Should I start with the first PR?
yes do A and B as separate PRs
Starting with PR A in its own worktree, since it changes behavior and needs the most care.

fix: reauth no longer refuses a slot overlap the configuration already had

Reauth checked every submitted lock against other entries' slots, so an
overlap on a lock the entry already holds refused every reauth, while the
options flow deliberately checks only added locks. Both now go through one
lock-change check, so they cannot drift apart again.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
git push -q -u origin HEAD 2>&1 | grep -v entire; gh pr create --title "fix: reauth no longer refuses a slot overlap the configuration already had" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Proposed change

If a lock in a configuration already shared a slot number with another configuration on the same lock, reauth refused with `slots_already_configured` every time, even when the user was only removing a lock that had gone away. The options flow already allows that overlap: it checks only the locks being *added*, and its comment says an existing overlap "must not refuse every later edit". Reauth ran its own copy of the same checks and passed every submitted lock instead.

Reauth and options now share one lock-change check (`_async_check_lock_change`), with the same order and the same `cannot_report` warning, so they can't drift apart again. `_check_common_slots` no longer needs its entry-exclusion parameter, because the locks being added never belong to the entry.

- Mutation check: changing the shared check back to examining every lock fails that test.
- `tests/test_config_flow.py`, `tests/test_init.py` and `tests/test_open_bugs.py`: 327 passed.

## Proposed change

Some Zigbee locks answer **Get PIN Code** for an empty index with a Default Response whose status is `NOT_FOUND` ("the requested table entry could not be found"), not with a Get PIN Code Response saying `Available`. The ZHA read treated that as a reply it couldn't parse and failed the whole read. Allocation then refused to add a user with `occupancy_unknown`, even though the lock had just said the slot holds nothing.

A Default Response to the read itself (naming `get_pin_code`) with status `NOT_FOUND` now reads as an empty slot. Any other Default Response, whether a different status or one naming another command, still fails the read as before. That keeps the existing rule that a reply nothing understood is never taken to mean the slot is free.

The design review (2026-10-11) moved this case to "model work" because the old credential model had no honest state for it. The clean-room core separates empty from cannot-tell, so it can be fixed now.
